title: Appeal to the saints' office as patrons proves the unknown by the equally unknown
source_text: XCIX. Quod si quis dicat officium Sanctis defunctis a Deo demandatum exigere ut rerum nostrarum notitiam habeant, quia scilicet, Patroni & intercessores nostri a Deo constituti sunt, ignotum probat per aeque ignotum. Nec enim Dei verbum ullibi docet Sanctos gloria caelesti fruentes a Deo nobis datos esse praesides & Mediatores, qui apud Deum pro nobis intercedant: imo contrarium satis evidenter ex Scriptura sacra colligitur. Nec etiam dici potest ad beatitudinem Sanctorum pertinere, ut audiant ipsos invocantium preces, quia nimirum hoc facit ad majorem eorum gloriam. Nam si Sanctorum in Christo defunctorum invocatio res superstitiosa atque illicita est, & ab hominibus tantum excogitata, ad gloriam Sanctorum nullo modo pertinet ut norint qui ipsos invocent: & prius probatum oportuit, Deo gratum & acceptum esse ut Sancti cum ipso regnantes invocentur, quam ut cum aliqua probabilitatis specie supponatur ejusmodi invocationem ad gloriam eorum facere.
pass_a_gloss: But if anyone says that the office entrusted by God to the departed Saints requires that they have knowledge of our affairs, because namely they have been constituted by God our Patrons and intercessors, he proves the unknown by the equally unknown. For the word of God nowhere teaches that the Saints enjoying heavenly glory have been given to us by God as guardians and Mediators, who intercede for us with God: rather the contrary is gathered quite evidently from sacred Scripture. Nor can it be said that it pertains to the blessedness of the Saints that they hear the prayers of those invoking them, because namely this makes for their greater glory. For if the invocation of Saints departed in Christ is a superstitious and unlawful thing, and devised only by men, it in no way pertains to the glory of the Saints that they know who invoke them: and it ought first to have been proved that it is pleasing and acceptable to God that the Saints reigning with him be invoked, before it is supposed with any appearance of probability that such invocation makes for their glory.
pass_b_english: Suppose someone says that the office God has given the departed saints requires them to know our affairs, since God has appointed them our patrons and intercessors. He proves the unknown by what is just as unknown.

God's word nowhere teaches that the saints who enjoy heavenly glory have been given us by God as guardians and mediators to intercede for us with him. On the contrary, the opposite is gathered quite clearly from Scripture.

Nor can it be said that hearing the prayers of those who call on them belongs to the saints' blessedness on the ground that it adds to their glory. If calling on the saints who have died in Christ is superstitious and unlawful, a human invention, then knowing who calls on them adds nothing to the saints' glory. It ought first to have been proved that God is pleased and accepts it when the saints who reign with him are invoked, before anyone could suppose with any show of probability that such invocation adds to their glory.

choices.why: Species is 'appearance'; Le Blanc denies the claim even a surface plausibility.
